steps.title: Five boards, the same five jobs
steps.body:
Each row is one board's boot chain; each column is one **job** that every chain has to do. Read a row left to right to follow a boot, or a column top to bottom to compare how the boards do the same job.

The dashed box is optional and not part of the default build.

steps.title: 1 · The Boot ROM is always the same job
steps.body: Fixed code inside the chip, run first, impossible to change. It reads the boot-mode setting and loads the next stage from the place the vendor chose: a fixed offset on the SD card, a named partition, a file in a FAT partition, or the module's on-board flash.

steps.title: 2 · The first loader trains the DRAM
steps.body: DRAM does not work at power-on, so a small program runs from on-chip RAM to bring it up. That is a tiny build of U-Boot (SPL) on the i.MX 8M Plus and the Zynq-7000, TF-A BL2 on both STM32 boards, and MB1 on the BPMP followed by MB2 on the Jetson.

steps.title: 3 · The secure world sits above Linux
steps.body: A secure monitor owns the highest privilege level and stays resident. Linux reaches it only through a narrow call interface. The STM32 boards require OP-TEE, because Linux asks it for clocks and resets; on the i.MX 8M Plus it is optional; the Jetson packages both in one NVIDIA image. The Zynq-7000 has none of it: its cores stay in the secure state.

steps.title: 4 · The bootloader hands over a device tree
steps.body: U-Boot (or UEFI on the Jetson) finds the kernel and the device tree, builds the kernel command line and jumps. Its last act is the same on every board: tell the kernel what hardware it is running on.

steps.title: 5 · Then it is just Linux
steps.body: The kernel mounts the root filesystem and starts user space. Everything you already know about Linux applies from here, which is why the root filesystem is the layer you can choose most freely.

steps.title: The Zynq-7000 row has no secure world
steps.body: Its first loader is a small build of the same U-Boot that later runs the board, and nothing sits above Linux. The board's memory and pin setup comes from a file generated by the FPGA vendor's tools (`ps7_init`), which is why that file is the part you have to get right for a new Zynq board.

steps.title: The Jetson row is the odd one out
steps.body: Its early stages run on small controllers and are stored in flash on the module, written by NVIDIA's tool, rather than on a card you assemble. That is the vendor-flash model; the other four rows are the SD-card model.

steps.title: Same jobs, different names
steps.body: When you meet a new SoC, look for these five jobs first. Once you know which stage does each, the vendor's names stop mattering.
